original_summary: Coyote is a bluffing and bidding game in the style of Indian poker. Each player sees every feather card except their own. Players take turns declaring ever-higher estimates of the total of all cards until someone calls 'Coyote'. The cards are then revealed: an over-declarer loses, otherwise the caller loses, and three losses eliminate a player.

review.evidence: Simple policies all lose. Always calling at once loses to any opener who declares low. Always raising by 1 is eventually caught over the true total. Always declaring very high is always caught. Every choice decides who takes the token. The only seat effect is who starts, and the starting rule ('the player who did not lose starts') ties the starting seat to past results.

The core reads (your hidden card from others' bids, the spread of the total) reward skill. But the blue specials add a lot of luck: 'add top of deck' and the reshuffle card can swing the total by up to 20 after all bidding is done, and nobody could have reasoned about it.

A weak player can still survive by bidding the visible sum plus the average card. A strong player keeps improving by reading what each opponent's bid implies about their own card, and by choosing between raising and calling depending on who acts after them.

Each player's own card is hidden from them and visible to everyone else, so the opponents' declarations are the only evidence about it. Doing well means inferring your card from bids and predicting whether later players will call.

The total is a sum with mechanical modifiers, and the loser follows by comparing it with the last declaration. Some blue-card rules ('discard highest positive' when ties exist, chains of specials) are underspecified and would need clarifying.

Bidding goes round the table an unbounded number of times, which breaks the limit of 4 choice steps per round. The five chained blue-card rules (including drawing extra cards and forced reshuffles) add several random draws in one round and long rule chains. With elimination at 3 tokens and up to 6 players, the game has no fixed length.

problems: P1: Bidding can circle the table any number of times, which exceeds the platform's limit of 4 choice steps per round.

P2: The five blue special cards (extra draw from the deck, discard highest, flip highest to negative, double positives, forced reshuffle) add post-bidding luck and extra random draws. They also form a long, partly ambiguous rule chain.
P3: Who starts depends on who lost, and elimination makes seats unequal: players do not hold the opening and closing positions equally often.
P4: The length is open-ended (elimination at 3 tokens with up to 6 players), and the game gets thin once few players remain.
P5: With up to 6 players, the number of hidden cards and turns per hand exceeds what fits in one round.

changes.what: Each hand is one round with exactly one lap of bidding. The opener declares, then each other player in clockwise order either raises or calls Coyote, once each. If nobody calls, the opener is automatically treated as calling Coyote on the final declaration.
changes.why: This bounds a hand at 4 choices while keeping the declare-or-call tension. The last responder can still dump the risk on someone else by raising only when confident, which keeps the late-position decision meaningful.

changes.what: The blue specials are replaced by one special card, 'Max→0': if it is in play, the highest other card counts as 0.
changes.why: This keeps Coyote's signature twist, which players can see and reason about because everyone else sees the card. It removes all post-bidding draws and reshuffles, so the outcome depends on reading, not on late luck.

changes.what: The game is a fixed 12 hands, and the opener rotates clockwise every hand, so each seat opens equally often (3 times with 4 players, 4 times with 3). Coyote tokens are counted and fewest tokens wins, instead of elimination.
changes.why: Every player holds every position (opener, middle, last responder) equally often, so no seat has an edge. The length is fixed and short.

changes.what: Elimination is dropped and the game ends after hand 12.
changes.why: This gives a bounded game length, and all players stay active and informative to the end.

changes.what: The player count is set to 3 or 4.
changes.why: The bidding lap fits within 4 choices, and there are enough visible cards to give real inference.

keeps: Each player sees every card except their own (the bandana).
Strictly rising declarations of the total of all cards in play.
Calling Coyote: an over-declaration costs the declarer, a correct declaration costs the caller.
Coyote tokens as the measure of losing.
Negative cards and the 'Max→0' special that makes the total tricky.
Reading your own card from what others are willing to declare.

recommendation.reason: The core (hidden own card, visible others, rising bids, a challenge) is strong inference and bluffing material. It only needs a bounded bidding lap, simpler specials and a symmetric fixed length to fit the platform.

variation.name: Coyote Lap
variation.summary: A Coyote game for 3 or 4 players over 12 hands. Each player sees every card but their own and bids on the total in a single lap: declare, raise or call Coyote. Whoever is wrong takes a token, and fewest tokens after 12 hands wins.
variation.rules:
DECK (33 cards): one -10, two -5, three 0, four each of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, three 10, two 15, one 20, and one special card 'Max→0'.

SETUP: Seat players in a fixed clockwise order. Each player starts with 0 Coyote tokens. The player in seat 1 opens hand 1. The game lasts exactly 12 hands.

EACH HAND:
1. Deal: shuffle the full 33-card deck and deal one card face down to each player.
2. Bandana: each player is told privately the cards of all other players, but never their own card.
3. Opening declaration: the opener declares a whole number from -30 to 60, a claim about the TRUE TOTAL of all cards in play this hand.
4. Responses: each other player, one at a time in clockwise order from the opener, chooses one of two options:
   (a) RAISE: declare a whole number strictly higher than the current declaration, at most 60. It becomes the current declaration, and this player becomes the current declarer.
   (b) CALL COYOTE: challenge the current declaration. Bidding stops immediately, and later players do not act this hand.
   Every declaration is announced to all players as it is made.
5. Automatic call: if every responder raised, the opener is treated as having called Coyote on the final declaration.
6. True total: add up the numbers on all cards in play. If the 'Max→0' card is in play, it counts as 0 itself, and the highest-valued other card in play also counts as 0. If several cards tie for highest, only one of them counts as 0. If the highest other card is negative, it still becomes 0.
7. Resolution: if the true total is LESS than the current declaration, the current declarer takes 1 Coyote token. Otherwise the caller, or the opener in the case of an automatic call, takes 1 Coyote token.
8. Reveal: all cards, the true total and the token taken are announced to everyone.
9. Rotate: the next player clockwise opens the next hand.

END: After hand 12, the game ends.
variation.objective: After 12 hands, the player with the fewest Coyote tokens wins. If two or more players tie for the fewest, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Each hand turns on two inferences. The first is estimating your own unseen card from how high the others are willing to go, since they can see it. The second is predicting whether players later in the lap will call or raise. The opener must declare near the true total: too low and everyone raises safely, leaving the opener stuck with the automatic call; too high and the next player calls. Middle players weigh calling now against passing the risk on. The last responder can raise by a small step only when confident, which shifts the risk onto the opener. Every seat holds every position equally often, so no seat has an edge. Removing post-bidding draws means the outcome follows from reading the bids, not from the deck. Free talk is deliberately left out. The declarations already carry the signal. Spoken claims about another player's card would be pure cheap talk in a contest only one player can win, so they would be ignored or add noise without giving anyone a new decision.

balanced.evidence:
DECK CHECK: 1+2+3+(4x5)+3+2+1+1 = 33 cards. Numeric sum = -10-10+0+4(1+2+3+4+5)+30+30+20 = 120, so the mean card is 3.75. E[x^2] = (100+50+220+300+450+400)/32 = 47.5, so the variance is 33.4 and the SD is about 5.8.

RANGE OF THE TRUE TOTAL T: maximum with 4 players is 20+15+15+10 = 60. Minimum is -10-5-5+0 = -20; with Max->0 it is -10,-5,-5,M = -15. The declaration range of -30 to 60 covers every possible T. A declaration of 60 leaves only CALL, which is legal.

WHO LOSES (3 players: Opener O, then A, then B, the last responder):
- B facing declaration d: CALL loses iff T>=d. RAISE to d+1 loses iff T<=d, because O auto-calls. B's only risk is guessing the wrong side.
- A facing d0: CALL loses iff T>=d0. RAISE exposes A to a call from B.
- O loses iff a responder calls while T<d0, or everyone raises and the final declaration is <= T.
So the last responder is structurally favoured and the opener is exposed. However, 12 hands rotate the opener through exactly 4 hands per seat with 3 players (12/3) or 3 per seat with 4 players (12/4). Every seat holds every position equally often, so there is no net seat edge.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule (fewest tokens; 12 tokens total, average 4 per player with 3, 3 with 4):
- Always open -30 / always call as responder: every responder raises by 1 at no risk (any d <= -20 is <= T). The opener is then auto-calling and loses 100% of opening hands, which is 4 tokens in 3p. As responder it loses whenever d <= T, roughly half the time against an opener who bids near the median, about 4 more. Total about 8 tokens against about 2 for each other player. LOSES.
- Always open 60 / always declare the maximum: the next player calls and wins unless T=60 exactly (under 0.1%). LOSES almost every time.
- Always raise by 1: a middle responder facing a high d0 (for example S+15) is pushed above T and gets called. Loses often, especially when sensible openers bid high to exploit it. LOSES on token count.
- Always call: covered above. LOSES.
- Random play: wrong-side errors cost about 50% of hands, against roughly 25-33% for informed play. LOSES.

DOMINANCE: no option is safe in every case.
- No opener declaration is safe. Low bids get raised safely, leaving the opener to auto-call. High bids get called.
- No responder choice is safe, because the responder's own card (SD 5.8) is unknown.

TIES: draws on tied fewest tokens will occur, but each player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS:
- The deal, private visibility of others' cards, the opening range, the raise bounds (strictly higher, at most 60) and the stop on CALL are all specified.
- The auto-call by the opener is defined.
- Resolution covers both the caller case and the auto-call case.
- Max->0 is fully specified: it counts as 0, exactly one highest other card is zeroed, ties zero only one, and a negative highest card still becomes 0. With 3 or more players there is always another card.
- At d=60 only CALL remains, and that option always exists.
- The original game's other blue specials (add top of deck, reshuffle) were removed, so no conditional deck sub-procedure is needed.

FINITE AND ARITHMETIC: the game is exactly 12 hands. Each hand ends after at most 1 opening and 3 responses. The winner is decided by an arithmetic count of fewest tokens.

LIMITS:
- choice steps: 1 opener + up to 3 responders = 4 (limit 4)
- steps: 12 (limit 20)
- attributes: 15 (limit 20)
- hidden elements: 1, the bandana card (limit 3)
- random draws per round: 1 shuffle-deal (limit 1)
- rounds: 12 (limit 40)

ENGINE SUPPORT:
- Sequential bidding uses sequential_choice and numeric_bids.
- The bandana uses hidden_hands / private_values, with each player shown the others' cards.
- The deal uses shared_deck_draw (workaround).
- The 'later players do not act' rule is per-step `when` conditions on a flat list, not a block substitution.
- No board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreements are needed.

TALK: there is no free talk. This is defensible: players are in strict conflict, and the declarations themselves are the signalling channel. Each bid encodes the bidder's view of other players' cards, including yours, so players reason from bids rather than blind guessing. Free talk would mostly add cheap lies about cards. The order of bidding is the point of the game, so sequential responses are appropriate.

REPEATED-GAME CHECK: there is no cooperate/defect structure, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SOURCE OF CHANCE: in each hand, a player's own card is unknown, with SD about 5.8 around a mean of 3.75 from that player's view. An uninformed estimate of T therefore has SD about 6.

INFERENCE CHANNEL: other players see your card, and their declarations encode it. Example with 3 players, where O sees A and B:
- A non-bluffing opener bids d0 ≈ A+B+3.75.
- B knows A, so B infers B ≈ d0 - A - 3.75.
- B then knows T almost exactly and can choose call or raise correctly.

So a careful listener can cut uncertainty close to zero. Good openers counter by shading and bluffing their declarations, and middle responders choose raise sizes that leak or hide information. This is genuine opponent modelling. Max->0 adds a known nonlinearity that players can reason about.

GOOD PLAY AGAINST WEAK PLAY: a model that ignores the bid information errs about 40-50% of the time on responder decisions. An inferring model errs far less. Over 12 hands this is a gap of several tokens, against a typical margin of 1-2 tokens between first and second place.

ALL PLAYERS PLAYING WELL: losses are concentrated on openers and middle responders, and position is rotated equally. The winner is decided by how well each player bluffs as opener and reads bids as responder, plus residual card noise. It is not decided by the deal alone, and no hidden type fixes the result.

ESTIMATE: chance accounts for roughly 35-45% of single-game outcomes. Reasoning is clearly favoured over 12 hands.
